criteria.note: The TL;DR block sits immediately under the update note and answers the 'celiac travel korea' intent — feasibility, anchor restaurants, the key phrase, store baseline — inside the first 200 words, followed immediately by a celiac-specific rules section.

Title is 35 chars (55 with the appended ' | Gluten-Free Korea'), description ~145 chars, keyword terms present in both, and the description covers distinct ground (phrases, labels, limits) rather than restating the title.

Headings carry argument rather than labels — 'If You're Celiac, Start Here', 'What Korean Food Actually Looks Like, From a Gluten Angle', 'The One Phrase That Actually Works' — and a heading-only skim yields the full thesis.
Seven-plus internal links, each placed where the reader would want the deeper resource (phrases post after the phrase section, label guide after the barley caveat, snacks post after the chip list).

All five FAQ answers are self-contained and each is backed by body text — the BBQ grill-contamination detail, the tamari caveat, the 237 Pizza unconfirmed status, and the 10%-wheat bakery anecdote all appear in the body.

Dense with dated, observed specifics: a franchise call in summer 2025, a shop closed for remodelling in summer 2026, a product silently renamed from 'gluten-free bread' to 'rice bread', and pink-vs-green packets of the same snack giving opposite label answers.
Korean terms are given with hangul plus romanisation and gloss (간장 ganjang, 어묵 eomuk, 쌀통닭 ssaltongdak, 원재료명), and named products (Goraesa, Poca Chip Original vs Onion, 참쌀설병) are checkable.

Primary sources carry retrieval or publication dates — the MFDS 식품등의 표시기준 link ('별표 2 — text in force as of August 2026'), Orion's own product page ('re-verified August 2026'), and the blogger roundup marked 'published October 2023' and explicitly demoted to a lead.

The piece repeatedly states what its method cannot establish ('our standard is NCGS, and we can't audit a kitchen'), retracts an unverifiable certification claim in the open, and contains no commercial or affiliate links requiring disclosure.

findings.quote: For long-term residents, traditional home-brewed soy sauce (집간장) without wheat is the classic option.
findings.why: The body establishes the underlying fact (the aunt brews wheat-free soy sauce the traditional way) but never uses the term 집간장 or frames it as the standing option for residents. If this FAQ renders as a rich result, the visible-content match Google expects is thin on that specific wording.
findings.fix: Add the term to the 'About My Wife' paragraph — e.g. 'traditional home-brewed soy sauce (집간장, jipganjang), made without wheat' — so the markup mirrors visible body text exactly.

findings.quote:
## In This Guide

1. **If you're celiac, start here** — the five stricter rules, up front
findings.why: The table of contents is plain text with no anchor links, so a reader who scans it still has to scroll manually to reach the section they picked. It also duplicates the H2 list without adding navigation value.
findings.fix: Convert each TOC entry to an in-page anchor link matching the H2 slugs, or drop the TOC since the descriptive headings already carry the skim.

findings.why: This is the only sibling post that never earns a contextual placement in the body — it appears solely in the end-of-post series dump, despite the 'What Korean Food Actually Looks Like, From a Gluten Angle' section being its natural anchor.
findings.fix: Link it inline at the close of the hidden-gluten tier list ('the full inventory of hidden sources is in ...'), which strengthens topical clustering for that section's keywords.

criteria.note: Nearly every claim is either sourced (MFDS, Orion, the dated blogger roundup) or explicitly framed as the authors' own field observation, but the 237 Pizza owner's medical history and founding motive are asserted flatly with no attribution — a non-safety-affecting unsourced claim.
criteria.evidence_quote: The owner has celiac disease himself, and opened 237 Pizza after years of research

criteria.note: Product names, store chains, brands, prices-free figures and all dates are checkable and internally consistent (April 2026 publication, August 2026 update, summer 2025 call correctly described as a year old, summer 2026 closure).

The piece states how it knows what it knows — visits, kitchen conversations, label reading, a dated phone call, a manufacturer page — and names what those methods cannot establish, including that it cannot audit a kitchen and that the non-Orion snack entries are third-party leads rather than verified findings.

No absolute safety guarantees survive unqualified, cross-contamination is raised at the grill, the shared kitchen, the shared fryer and the shared production line, and celiac risk is consistently escalated above the authors' NCGS standard rather than flattened into it.

Every source carries a retrieval or publication date, the 2023 blogger roundup is flagged as stale and demoted to a lead, the 2025 franchise call has its elapsed year stated, and the reformulation-without-notice risk is called out explicitly.

The labelling law is described correctly, including the wheat-only mandatory scope, but the claim that tteokbokki rice cakes are inherently gluten-free is wrong for Korea, where wheat-flour tteok (밀떡) is common in both street stalls and retail packets.
criteria.evidence_quote: the rice cakes themselves are GF, but the sauce contains gochujang and the fish cakes mixed in have wheat

criteria.note: The reader is given the primary legal text, a manufacturer allergen page, the exact Korean words to scan for, and a staff reconfirmation script, so no safety-relevant claim requires taking the author's word.

findings.quote: the rice cakes themselves are GF, but the sauce contains gochujang and the fish cakes mixed in have wheat
findings.why: Korean tteok is not reliably rice-only. Wheat-flour tteokbokki tteok (밀떡) is widespread at street stalls, franchises and in supermarket packets, and is often preferred for its texture. A celiac reader who takes 'the rice cakes themselves are GF' as a category fact could buy packaged tteok, or order a sauce-free/custom tteokbokki, and eat wheat. The surrounding advice to avoid tteokbokki blunts but does not remove the exposure, since the sentence generalises about the ingredient rather than the dish.
findings.fix: Replace with something like: 'Tteok comes in both rice (쌀떡) and wheat (밀떡) versions — street and franchise tteokbokki frequently uses 밀떡 — so the rice cake is not a safe assumption. Check 원재료명 on packaged tteok and ask 쌀떡인가요, 밀떡인가요? before ordering. The sauce (gochujang) and the fish cakes are separate wheat sources on top of that.'

findings.quote: The owner has celiac disease himself, and opened 237 Pizza after years of research
findings.why: A specific medical claim about a named, identifiable business owner is presented as established fact with no attribution and no marker that it came from a conversation at the shop. It does not drive a safety decision on its own, but on a site where 'the owner is celiac' functions as an implicit trust signal, its provenance should be visible — especially in a passage where an adjacent certification claim has already had to be withdrawn.
findings.fix: Attribute it to its actual origin, e.g. 'The owner told us he has celiac disease himself and opened the shop after years of research' — or drop it if it came from secondhand reporting the authors cannot re-confirm.

findings.quote: A GF cafe with gorgeous cakes — strawberry, chocolate, seasonal fruit — on the second floor of the Magok Sciencestar Building. Most of the menu is gluten-free.
findings.why: benir is placed in Tier 2 (GF-friendly, not dedicated) yet is opened with the bare label 'A GF cafe', which collides with the article's own Tier 1 definition and with the following sentence admitting only 'most' of the menu is GF and that some toppings may contain gluten. A skimming celiac reader could carry the Tier 1 anchor logic to a shared-kitchen venue. This does not cost a rubric point because the paragraph discloses the gluten-containing items in the very next line, but the opening phrase should not do work the venue has not earned.
findings.fix: Change the opener to 'A GF-focused cafe (not dedicated — shared kitchen)' so the tier label and the description agree on first read.
